report.headline: The ACCELERATE trial of evacetrapib was stopped for futility in ~12,092 high-risk vascular patients, confirming that CETP inhibition does not reduce cardiovascular events despite large HDL-C increases.
report.summary: The ACCELERATE trial randomized 12,092–12,095 patients with high-risk vascular disease to evacetrapib 130 mg or placebo on background statin therapy. The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularization, or hospitalization for unstable angina, with 1,670 planned events. The independent data monitoring committee stopped the trial early on October 12, 2015, for insufficient efficacy with no safety signal. Evacetrapib produced massive HDL-C elevations (+129% within-arm, +103% placebo-adjusted) and modest LDL-C lowering (~‑15% placebo-adjusted), but the calculator predicted only a 37% probability of success (expected HR 0.923) based on the LDL-C effect, yielding 37% power (MDE HR 0.872 for 80% power). Human genetics available at trial launch showed a CETP association score of 0.736 but zero supporting studies before the 2015 cutoff, indicating HDL-C is not a causal mediator for coronary disease. The failure aligns with the primary category biomarker_not_causal (HDL-C non-causal), with secondary contributions from effect_too_small (LDL-C lowering below detection threshold) and target_not_causal (uncertain CETP genetics at launch).
key_evidence: 12,092–12,095 patients randomized (Lilly to Discontinue Development of Evacetrapib for High-Risk Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (Oct 12, 2015); ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01687998 ACCELERATE; Assessment of the clinical effects of cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibition with evacetrapib in patients at high-risk for vascular outcomes: Rationale and design of the ACCELERATE trial)

1,670 planned primary endpoint events (Assessment of the clinical effects of cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibition with evacetrapib in patients at high-risk for vascular outcomes: Rationale and design of the ACCELERATE trial)

Primary endpoint composite: CV death, MI, stroke, coronary revascularization, hospitalization for unstable angina (Assessment of the clinical effects of cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibition with evacetrapib in patients at high-risk for vascular outcomes: Rationale and design of the ACCELERATE trial; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01687998 ACCELERATE)
Trial stopped early by DSMB for futility on Oct 12, 2015, no safety signal (Lilly to Discontinue Development of Evacetrapib for High-Risk Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (Oct 12, 2015))

Phase 2/3 HDL-C increase: +129% within-arm at 130 mg (Assessment of the clinical effects of cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibition with evacetrapib in patients at high-risk for vascular outcomes: Rationale and design of the ACCELERATE trial); +103% placebo-adjusted vs atorvastatin alone (Efficacy, safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetic profile of evacetrapib administered as monotherapy or in combination with atorvastatin in Japanese patients with dyslipidemia)

Placebo-adjusted LDL-C lowering ~‑15% (0.56 mmol/L) in phase 2 combination data (Efficacy, safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetic profile of evacetrapib administered as monotherapy or in combination with atorvastatin in Japanese patients with dyslipidemia)
Calculator predicted 37% probability of success (HR 0.923, 7.7% RRR) with 37% power (MDE HR 0.872 for 80% power) based on LDL-C reduction (calculator)
CETP genetic association score 0.736 but zero genetic evidence items before 2015‑10‑12 cutoff (opentargets:CETP)

No QT prolongation at supratherapeutic dose (Evacetrapib at a supratherapeutic steady state concentration does not prolong QT in a thorough QT/QTc study in healthy participants); no clinically relevant blood pressure effects (Effects of the cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitor evacetrapib on lipoproteins, apolipoproteins and 24-h ambulatory blood pressure in healthy adults)
report.what_would_change_this: A pre‑2015 Mendelian randomization study showing that lifelong CETP inhibition raising HDL-C reduces coronary risk would have supported target causality; a larger placebo‑adjusted LDL‑C reduction at the trial dose (e.g., >‑25%) would have increased the expected treatment effect above the trial's detection threshold.
report.readthrough_note: Other CETP inhibitors have shown mixed results: torcetrapib increased mortality (off‑target toxicity), dalcetrapib was neutral, while anacetrapib demonstrated modest cardiovascular benefit attributed to LDL‑C lowering rather than HDL‑C elevation. The ACCELERATE outcome reinforces that CETP inhibition per se does not translate into clinical benefit via HDL‑C raising.

mechanism.target_genetics_rationale: CETP genetic association score 0.736 for CAD but all 13 Open Targets studies published after 2015-10-12 cut-off (evidence_before_cutoff=0). No genetic evidence before cut-off for this well-studied target -> uncertain.

for.text: Evacetrapib is a CETP inhibitor developed to raise HDL-C; phase 2 combination data show +103% HDL-C vs active comparator (atorvastatin alone) at 100 mg + atorvastatin 10 mg (12 weeks), and phase 3 within-arm data show +129% and +54% HDL-C at the trial dose of 130 mg.

Human genetics do not support HDL-C as a causal mediator for coronary artery disease; CETP genetic association score is 0.736 but all 13 supporting studies were published after the 2015-10-12 cutoff (evidence_before_cutoff: 0), meaning no genetic evidence supported CETP/HDL-C causality at trial launch.

The calculator's intended_biomarker is HDL-C, and the drug moved this biomarker as planned (massive elevation), yet the trial failed for insufficient efficacy — the classic signature of a non-causal biomarker.

hypotheses.would_settle: Mendelian randomization studies of CETP variants on CVD outcomes (published after 2015) confirm that lifelong CETP inhibition raising HDL-C does not reduce coronary risk.

for.text: At the trial dose (130 mg), phase 3 within-arm LDL-C reductions were -14% and -36%; the calculator used a -15% LDL-C change (from phase 2 combination data vs active comparator) yielding an expected HR of 0.923 (7.7% RRR) with only 37% power to detect it (MDE HR 0.872 for 80% power).

Phase 2 monotherapy placebo-adjusted LDL-C lowering was -23% at 100 mg (12 weeks), suggesting the true placebo-adjusted effect at 130 mg may be in the -15% to -25% range — still yielding expected HR ~0.90-0.93, below the trial's detection threshold.

against.text: The -15% LDL-C input (f_58aadd0f20c7b8) was flagged by the verifier as not_found in the abstract; it described monotherapy vs placebo, not combination with atorvastatin. The true placebo-adjusted LDL-C effect at the trial dose on background statin is uncertain.

hypotheses.would_settle: Placebo-adjusted LDL-C change at 130 mg on background statin therapy from the ACCELERATE trial itself (not yet published at cutoff).

for.text: CETP genetic association score is 0.736 but evidence_before_cutoff is 0 (all 13 studies post-2015); at the time of trial design (2012) and launch, human genetics did not support CETP as a causal target for CVD.
The calculator's target_genetics is 'uncertain' (not 'negative'), and its weakest_link is 'target genetics: uncertain'.

against.text: Genetic evidence accumulated after 2015 (e.g., CETP loss-of-function variants) shows neutral or modest effects on CVD, not strongly protective — consistent with 'uncertain' rather than definitively 'not causal' at trial launch.

hypotheses.would_settle: Pre-2015 Mendelian randomization or genetic studies of CETP and CVD (none existed per evidence_before_cutoff=0).

for.text: Primary endpoint composite included coronary revascularization and hospitalization for unstable angina — softer endpoints that may dilute a treatment effect on hard atherosclerotic events.
Median follow-up was only 1.5 years (event-driven but stopped early); CETP inhibition's benefit on atherosclerosis progression might require longer exposure.

against.text: The trial was event-driven (planned 1670 events) and randomized 12,092 patients; the composite is standard for CV outcome trials and the hard components (CV death, MI, stroke) would capture mechanistic benefit if it existed.

hypotheses.would_settle: Component-specific hazard ratios from the final ACCELERATE publication (post-cutoff).

for.text: Supratherapeutic dose (600 mg, Day 14) showed a +1.69 mmHg SBP increase (placebo-adjusted).

against.text: Phase 2 readout explicitly states evacetrapib was 'devoid of clinically relevant effects on blood pressure and mineralocorticoid levels' at 600 mg Day 14.
No QT prolongation at 1200 mg daily (supratherapeutic).
Safety signals were negative across phase 2 and phase 3; the trial was stopped for futility, not harm.

hypotheses.would_settle: Blood pressure data from the ACCELERATE trial at the therapeutic dose (130 mg) on background statin.

for.text: High-risk vascular disease patients on intensive statin background therapy; residual events may be driven by non-lipid pathways (inflammation, thrombosis) unaffected by CETP inhibition.

against.text: If LDL-C lowering were causal, benefit should still accrue in this population (as seen with statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors on statin background).

hypotheses.would_settle: Subgroup analyses by baseline LDL-C, statin intensity, or event type from the final trial data.

for.text: Trial stopped early for futility by independent data monitoring committee (sponsor announcement).

against.text: Stopping for futility is a consequence of the biological null result, not an independent execution failure; recruitment (12,092) and event accrual proceeded as planned.

hypotheses.would_settle: Data monitoring committee charter and interim analysis plan.

against.text: Substantial verified data exist: genetics, biomarker changes (phase 2 and phase 3), trial design, sample size, events, follow-up, and outcome.

Randomized controlled trial conducted among 398 patients with elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) or low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels from April 2010 to January 2011 at community and academic centers in the United States and Europe.
The study enrolled 76 subjects (52 (68%) African-Americans; 22 (29%) Caucasians; 2 (3%) Asians), with a mean (± standard deviation (SD)) age of 36.8 (±9.6) years (range 21–60 years).
